name: Pull-ups

lead:
A pull-up is an upper-body strength exercise: you hang from a bar and pull until your elbows reach your torso. It works the latissimus dorsi, trapezius and biceps.[1]
For looks, lat development is what gives the back width and the V-taper that makes shoulders look broader against the waist. Users on looksmax.org call pull-ups the best exercise for back width.[2]

paras: Variations include chin-ups (underhand grip), wide grips, weighted pull-ups with a belt or vest, assisted versions with bands, and eccentric lowering as a progression for people who cannot yet do one.[1][2] Lifters add weight once bodyweight reps are easy.[2]

Overhead pulling can narrow the subacromial space and risk shoulder impingement; one study found a pronated grip at shoulder width carried less impingement risk than other variations tested. Kipping pull-ups are a major cause of shoulder injury among CrossFit athletes.[1]

chain: Pull bodyweight (or added load) up to a bar
Lats and upper back grow with training
angle.text: Regular pull-up training builds the lats and surrounding upper-back muscles, which widen the back and exaggerate the shoulder-to-waist ratio. Progression through variations and added weight is the usual route.

lead: A pull-up is a closed-chain compound exercise in which the body hangs from a bar and is pulled up until the elbows reach the torso, using an overhand, underhand, neutral or rotating grip. The primary muscles are the latissimus dorsi, trapezius and biceps brachii.[1] The lats are a large, fan-shaped back muscle running from the lower spine and pelvis to the upper arm bone, and a developed pair is what gives a back its width.[2]

In looksmaxxing and physique communities, pull-ups are valued for building lat width, which contributes to the V-shaped upper body: broad back and shoulders tapering to a narrower waist. A looksmax.org thread argues that no single exercise is on par for back growth and width, and advises a linear progression until a first pull-up and then added weight to keep progressing.[3] The chain people describe is simple: a harder pull-up variation, more lat and upper-back muscle over months of training, and a wider-looking frame in a T-shirt or at the beach.

Pull-ups also serve as a fitness benchmark: they measure upper-body strength, endurance and strength-to-weight ratio and are used in job fitness tests for firefighting, policing and the military.[1] Users trade counts in forums, such as a thread asking how many pull-ups people can do in a row.[4] The oldest source cited in Wikipedia's article is a 1932 commentary.[1]

paras: The lowering phase ends in a full dead hang, and the top position may be chin over the bar or higher, as in the chest-to-bar version.[1] Grips are typically 20 to 50 percent wider than shoulder width in studies where participants chose their own grip; overly wide grips may raise injury risk or reduce repetitions.[1] A chin-up uses an underhand (supinated) grip, a mixed grip has one hand each way, and equipment can be a bar, a doorway bar, towels, rotating handles or gymnastic rings.[1]

subs.h: Progressions for people who cannot yet do one
paras: Assisted versions use bands, counterweights or foot support, and eccentric pull-ups lower slowly from the top to a dead hang as a way to build toward a first repetition.[1] The looksmax.org thread above points to a bodyweight-progression guide that moves through close-grip, wide-grip, archer and sternum-level variations.[3] Wikipedia cites a 2003 study in which about one third of college-age women completed a pull-up after a twelve-week full-body strength programme.[1]

Weighted pull-ups add load with a dip belt or vest and are the usual route once bodyweight repetitions become easy.[1][3] One-arm and one-finger versions exist, and the muscle-up, which transitions into a dip, originates in gymnastics.[1] Kipping pull-ups use momentum, show lower upper-body and higher lower-body and core activation, and are described as a major cause of shoulder injury among CrossFit athletes.[1]

Early in the movement the trapezius, infraspinatus and brachialis are most active; the lats, teres major and biceps peak mid-pull, and the triceps and subscapularis peak at the top.[1] A 2017 study found a pronated grip activated the middle trapezius more than a neutral grip, though overall activation across grips was similar.[1] The lats adduct, extend and internally rotate the shoulder, and with the arms fixed overhead they pull the trunk up toward the hands. Anatomy references list pull-ups, chin-ups and pull-downs among vertical pulls for the muscle, alongside straight-arm pulldowns, pullovers and deadlifts.[2]
A 2022 study reported that performing repetitions in a set without resting at the bottom is more efficient because of stretch-shortening rebound in muscle and tendon.[1]

The V-taper is the ratio of upper-body width to waist width. Lat training widens the back below the shoulders, and the muscle's insertion on the upper arm gives the back a flared outline from the front and rear. Forum users describe pull-ups as the main lat builder in a bodyweight-only routine, and some combine them with rows and overhead pressing for shoulder width.[3]

Lifters in these communities commonly track progress by repetition counts and added load rather than measurements: one poster reports 22 in a row and jokes that long legs are a handicap, while another lists a record of 16 with imperfect technique.[4]

Overhead movements can narrow the subacromial space and risk shoulder impingement; a 2016 study reported that a pronated, shoulder-width grip carried less impingement risk than other variations tested.[1] Kipping pull-ups are described as high risk.[1] A Hacker News thread discusses a 2019 study suggesting push-ups and pull-ups as an alternative to surgery for rotator cuff pain.[5] Tight lats have been linked to shoulder and back pain in anatomy references, and lat injuries are rare but occur more often in baseball pitchers.[2]

Guinness World Records lists Kenta Adachi of the Japan Coast Guard with 651 consecutive pull-ups in 2022 and 1,224 in 2024 under a rule of one every 15 seconds, and Liu Weiqiang with a 146.64 kg weighted pull-up in China in 2025.[1] Some organisations let women substitute a flexed-arm hang in fitness tests because few female recruits could do a pull-up.[1] Pull-up numbers also serve as conditioning markers for climbing, gymnastics, rope climbing, rowing and swimming.[1]

On looksmax.org, users describe pull-ups as a core back exercise, share progression plans from close grip to archer variations, and post max-rep numbers.[3][4] Another thread discusses weighted pull-ups in the context of perceived hormonal effects.[6]

No studies found of pull-ups specifically for back width or appearance. Systematic reviews of related topics exist, such as deltoid activation during strengthening exercises and body composition in sport climbers.[7][8]
